stances.claim: The Revised Guidelines for Continuous Trial of Criminal Cases are a formidable and well-designed tool that will indeed hasten criminal trials.
Provision 2 -- outright denial of prohibited motions before arraignment without comment or opposition -- is a decisive break from the culture of endless motion-filing by enterprising lawyers.
stances.rhetorical_move: identification of the most transformative single provision

stances.claim: Provision 5 -- allowing multiple accused to adopt prior evidence (as in the Maguindanao massacre) -- saves 'valuable time in presenting anew the witnesses and documents already taken up in the existing case.'
The RGs are limited to criminal cases and do not address all the causes of delay -- a comprehensive reform covering civil and administrative cases is still needed.

notable_anecdotes: Sen. Gringo Honasan's P29.1M pork barrel case becoming the first SBN citation of the new RGs -- a quash bid and MR both rejected using the guidelines.
The Maguindanao massacre cited as the paradigm case for Provision 5's multiple-accused evidence adoption -- its long-pending status illustrating exactly why the adoption shortcut is necessary.
The fill-in-the-blanks templates (Provision 9) -- a rare procedural innovation that removes the 'no time to prepare pleadings' excuse from lawyers and judges alike.
The 77% criminal-case composition of 600,000+ pending trial court/SBN/CTA cases -- contextualizing why the RGs' criminal-cases-only scope is still a major step.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the Revised Guidelines for Continuous Trial of Criminal Cases (RGs), prompted by the Sandiganbayan's Second Division (JJ Herrera Jr., Musngi, and Pahimna) citing them to reject Sen. Gringo Honasan's bid to quash his P29.1 million pork barrel case. The RGs, effective September 1, 2017 as a supplement to the Rules of Court, were drafted by Justice Diosdado M. Peralta's Special Committee to address 600,000+ pending criminal cases (77% of all trial court/SBN/CTA dockets). At 56 pages with annexes, the nine key provisions are: (1) continuous morning-and-afternoon hearings Monday through Thursday, with Fridays reserved for motions, arraignment, and promulgation; (2) prohibited motions denied outright before arraignment without comment or opposition; (3) postponements allowed only for force majeure or physical inability of a witness; (4) IBP local chapters provide counsels de officio to remove lack-of-counsel as a postponement ground; (5) multiple accused may adopt prior evidence rather than re-presenting it (Maguindanao massacre as example); (6) rereading of the information may be waived with the accused's consent; (7) plea bargaining proceeds immediately with proper consents, followed by immediate judgment; (8) a flow chart sets 180 days for evidence presentation (60 in drug cases) and 90 days for decision (15 in drug cases); and (9) fill-in-the-blanks templates preempt the excuse of not having prepared pleadings and orders on time. The author endorses the RGs as an effective tool for hastening criminal trials but notes their limit: they cover only criminal cases, and a comprehensive series of reforms is still needed for civil and administrative proceedings.
